idiom_name: remote contract abstraction + local stand-in + one selection seam (Gateway/interface plus factory, plugin or link seam)
implementation_notes: Language-neutral form: (1) name the remote service as an abstraction the client holds (PoEAA's Gateway) - operations, types and error semantics - and forbid the client from reaching the transport directly; (2) provide a second implementation that answers from canned or scripted data, in memory, with no network; (3) select the implementation in exactly one place - constructor injection, a factory or plugin, a DI registration, a build or link configuration, or the RPC runtime that binds a generated stub to a channel; (4) bound the stand-in's fidelity with the published contract (IDL, OpenAPI, recorded interactions) and re-verify it with contract tests against the real service, because a stand-in nobody checks becomes fiction. The classic form stays justified whenever the remote is third-party, unavailable, metered or slow; where the dependency can be run locally, prefer the real thing.
code_sketch:
interface PriceService:                     # the remote contract (Gateway)
    price(sku) -> Money

class RemotePriceService(PriceService): ... # production: dials the service
class StubPriceService(PriceService):       # local: canned, in memory
    def price(self, sku): return self.canned[sku]

client = Checkout(service=stub if offline else remote)  # one seam
pitfalls: Letting the client branch on which implementation it holds (if test: ...) - the seam has leaked and the stand-in now shapes production logic.
A stand-in that answers with something the remote never returns (permissive defaults, invented fields), so the client is validated against a contract that does not exist.
No contract check against the live service: the stand-in silently becomes the specification.
Shipping the stand-in - it must not be reachable from a production build path or switchable by a runtime flag.

Wrong move: the stand-in re-implements the remote's business rules (pricing, eligibility, rounding) so client tests have rich answers -> the rules drift the first time the real service changes and both sides still test green -> keep the stand-in data-driven and thin: canned payloads lifted from captured real responses, logic owned only by the real service.

Wrong move: every collaborator down the call chain gets a stand-in, layer upon layer -> the suite pins an invented architecture and passes while no real layer has ever run -> double only the external boundary and let internal collaborators run for real.

Wrong move: the team points its tests at a shared staging environment instead of maintaining local stand-ins -> tests inherit other teams' deploys, seeded data and outages, and failure paths still cannot be produced on demand -> keep local stubs for logic tests and reserve the staging environment for deliberate integration runs.
